lead: A navigation controller owns a stack of view controllers. The bottom is the root; new screens are pushed on top. A segue is a storyboard-declared move from one screen to another. It pushes inside a navigation controller, or presents modally, and carries data through prepare(for:sender:). This gives the back button, titles and a predictable return path. Most UIKit apps use this for list and detail screens. Only a few universities teach segues in detail.
prereq: You need: a source screen with data and a destination screen to fill from Chapter 6.5 and Chapter 6.6.

blocks.text: UINavigationController is a container view controller. It shows one child at a time and remembers a stack. The first screen is the root view controller. The root stays loaded at the bottom. Push a new view controller to slide it on top. Pop removes the top controller and reveals the one below. The navigation bar shows the current title and a back button. Set title for short text. Set navigationItem.largeTitleDisplayMode on each screen, and navigationController?.navigationBar.prefersLargeTitles once for the whole stack. The back button is created for you and labelled with the previous screen's title.
Use pushViewController(_:animated:) and popViewController(animated:) in code. Storyboards create the same pushes through a show segue.

A segue is a storyboard connection from a control or cell to a destination scene. A show segue pushes only when the source is inside a UINavigationController. Outside one, UIKit falls back to modal presentation: the destination appears without a back button or navigation bar. To get a push, embed the source in a UINavigationController. Present Modally also shows the destination over the current screen, with no back button; add a Close button that calls dismiss(animated:). An unwind segue goes backwards to an existing screen by calling an @IBAction method that takes a UIStoryboardSegue.

items: Give the segue an identifier, for example showDetail.
Call performSegue(withIdentifier: "showDetail", sender: self), or let the cell tap trigger it.
Override prepare(for:sender:). Read sender or tableView.indexPathForSelectedRow in the source controller.
Cast segue.destination as? DetailViewController; if nil, return.
Set destination properties, for example detail.fare = 158.

blocks.text: On a push, the destination runs viewDidLoad once, then viewWillAppear and viewDidAppear. When you pop back, the source's viewWillAppear fires again. Its viewDidLoad does not run again. Use viewWillAppear to refresh values that may change while Detail is open.

blocks.output: Result: row 1 sets detail.fare to 158 before Detail appears; prepare returns no value.

sections.h3: Tab bar controllers and safe data passing

blocks.text: A UITabBarController switches between whole view controllers or whole navigation stacks. Each tab keeps its own stack and root. Tapping a tab selects a child; it does not push. Apps use this for Home, Bookings and Account. Some syllabi list tab bar controllers and the view controller life cycle with this chapter.

For a storyboard segue, prepare(for:sender:) is the correct place to hand data over. For a code-driven push, create the destination, set its properties, then call pushViewController(_:animated:). An initializer or closure is also valid. prepare(for:sender:) runs before the destination appears, so outlets may not be connected yet. Read tableView.indexPathForSelectedRow in the source controller inside prepare, because the source owns the table view. The row stays selected after you return unless you call tableView.deselectRow(at:animated:) yourself. Use as? and a guard. A wrong identifier or class then does nothing instead of crashing. Force-casting with as! is the usual crash in exams.

figure.caption: Tapping row 1 runs prepare, which sets detail.fare to ₹158, and the push takes the stack from one screen to two. Back pops Detail and returns to the same fare list.

spec.aria: A four-step flow for the fare list example: tapping row 1, prepare setting detail.fare to 158, pushing Detail so the stack grows from 1 to 2 controllers, and Back popping Detail while the list stays unchanged.

examples.question: A fare list shows fares ₹92, ₹158 and ₹65. The user taps row index 1. A show segue with identifier showDetail runs. (a) What fare is passed? (b) What are the stack contents before and after? (c) What changes if the same screen is presented modally instead?
steps: Store the fares in order: fares = [92, 158, 65] rupees. Index 1 is the second row.
Read the selected row: fare = fares[1] = ₹158.
In prepare(for:sender:), cast destination as? DetailViewController and set detail.fare = 158.
Before the push the stack has 1 controller, [Fare List]. After the push it has 2, [Fare List, Detail].
The back button pops Detail and the list is unchanged. Modal presentation has no back button; add Close calling dismiss.
examples.answer: The detail screen receives ₹158; the stack grows from 1 to 2 controllers, [Fare List, Detail]. Modal presentation removes the automatic back button.
examples.check:
fares = [92, 158, 65]
selected_row = 1
fare = fares[selected_row]
stack_before = 1
stack_after = stack_before + 1
print(fare)
print(stack_after)

traps: Reading tableView.indexPathForSelectedRow in the destination: the destination has no access to the source table view. Read it in the source inside prepare(for:sender:). The row stays selected after you return unless you deselect it.
Force-casting segue.destination as! DetailViewController with a wrong identifier or class crashes. Use as? and return on nil.

Using a show segue outside a navigation controller: UIKit falls back to modal presentation. The screen appears but has no back button or navigation bar. Embed the source in a UINavigationController for a push.
Confusing viewDidLoad with viewWillAppear: when you pop back, viewWillAppear runs again, viewDidLoad does not.

quiz.q: Which class keeps a stack of view controllers?
How does a show segue differ from Present Modally?
quiz.a: Show pushes inside a navigation controller and gets a back button. Outside one it falls back to modal presentation. Modal shows the destination over the current screen with no automatic back button.

quiz.q: A navigation stack has root A, then pushes B and C. What is the stack, and what does pop return?
quiz.a: The stack is [A, B, C]. pop returns C and reveals B.

quiz.q: Why should prepare(for:sender:) use as? and not as! when casting the destination?
quiz.a: A wrong storyboard class or identifier makes as! crash. as? returns nil, so a guard can stop safely instead of crashing the app.

quiz.q: Which table view property gives the selected row before a segue?
How is a tab bar controller different from a navigation controller?
quiz.a: A tab bar controller switches between whole children or whole stacks. A navigation controller pushes and pops screens inside one stack.

beyond: Not for the exam. UIKit segues still appear in maintenance code and older tutorials. New app projects often use SwiftUI NavigationStack and NavigationLink instead, which declare navigation in code. The idea of a stack and of passing data at the moment of transition still applies. Search for UINavigationController documentation, prepare(for:sender:), and SwiftUI NavigationStack to compare.
